winner.title: Grilled Barramundi Recipe

evidence.authenticity: US blogger; plain direct-heat grilling of barramundi, which is recognizably the dish, but the avocado-orange salsa is a modern American topping. Intro notes barramundi is an Australian favorite. No Australian authorship or regional context.
evidence.precision: Fillet size given (6 oz, 1 inch thick, 2-3 inches wide); salt 1/2 tsp per fillet; 145 F internal temp; 5 sensory cues (browned bottom, opaque in thickest part, check along seams with paring knife, skin protects fish); gas and charcoal setups described; no gram weights.
evidence.testing: Author explains why (oil the grate, skin side protects flesh, how to test doneness). Single author, no test kitchen; 1 rating.
evidence.photos: 52 images on page, but WebFetch returned 403 so process photos could not be confirmed. Scored on the image count only.
evidence.efficiency: 36 minutes total; the salsa is made while the grill preheats. The 15-minute preheat is described.
evidence.access: Barramundi is sold frozen at US grocers (Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, Costco). No substitute given, but any firm white fish would work. Everything else is common.

winner.why: It had the highest Precision of the candidates (internal temp, thickness, doneness cues), but it is a Westernized preparation and its score is under 60 once authenticity and unconfirmed photos are counted.

runnerUp.title: Paperbark barramundi with lemon myrtle butter
runnerUp.source: SBS Food (Samantha Martin, Bush Tukka Woman)

evidence.authenticity: Written by an Indigenous Australian bush-food expert; whole baby barramundi on the barbecue with paperbark and lemon myrtle, a genuinely Australian method.
evidence.precision: Fish weight given (550-650 g), butter 40 g; time-based steps (10 min, turn, 10 min) with 'until cooked through' as the only cue; no temperatures; rice step has a missing number ('a further minutes').
evidence.testing: Expert author, but no reasoning for steps. Not a test kitchen.
evidence.photos: No step images in schema; 12 images on the page, probably hero and promotional.
evidence.efficiency: Rice cooks while the fish is prepped; 40 minutes total.
evidence.access: Paperbark, lemon myrtle and lemon aspen are hard to find in the US. Foil and baking paper alone would do for wrapping, but no substitutes are given.

runnerUp.why: Most authentic of the candidates, but time-only steps and hard-to-find paperbark and lemon myrtle with no substitutes kept it below the winner.

candidates.disqualified: Southeast Asian style (makrut lime, shaoxing, soy), not a traditional Australian grilled barramundi; single paragraph step
No weights for the fish, vague times, inconsistent ingredient/step (flowers vs leaves), one photo; needs native plants (karkalla, saltbush)
No Recipe structured data; retailer blog, not scored

searches: Australian barbecued barramundi whole fish lemon myrtle butter
notes: No candidate reached 60. Serious Eats and NYT had nothing on barramundi; the NYT hit was striped bass. The best Australian-authored recipes (SBS, Tucker Bush) are time-only and need paperbark or lemon myrtle. Only 7 recipes were read successfully, from 5 sites. No native-language search was run because the dish is English-named. A RETRY could look for an RecipeTin Eats or Taste.com.au barramundi recipe, or a Gourmet Traveller one (https://www.gourmettraveller.com.au/recipe/chefs-recipes/barramundi-8073/ appeared in search but was not read). A simple Australian-style fillet with lemon and herb butter would likely score above 60.
